text: The last three lessons got you into the room with a well-structured argument, prepared for the likely questions, and able to defend a tradeoff you made on purpose. This lesson is about what happens once the meeting actually ends -- because a real review almost never produces a simple 'approved, go build it.'

It produces one of three outcomes. Approved means the design proceeds as presented -- the simplest outcome, and the least common one for anything substantive. Approved with conditions means the direction is accepted, but specific items, like a documented rollback path, have to be addressed before or during build. And revise and return means real rework is needed, tied to one specific, named concern -- the blast radius is too wide, or the cost model breaks at the stated scale. None of these are a rejection of the effort; they're the review process catching a real problem before it gets built instead of after.

Not every comment in a review is a change request. Reviewers process information live, and a point you already made sometimes gets restated as if it were new. The discipline afterward is sorting feedback into two piles: things genuinely not considered, which change the design, and things already addressed, which just need to be restated more clearly next time. Treating every comment as equally binding is how a design drifts away from its original intent, one unnecessary change at a time.

Revising well means going back to the original problem statement before touching the design, since feedback is only valid relative to the problem you were actually solving. It means changing only what the specific feedback requires -- a rollback-path condition isn't a license to redesign the network topology too. And it means updating the ADR's consequences section, not just the diagram, so the record of why the design looks the way it does now includes the feedback that shaped it.

When the revised design goes back to the board, open with what they asked for and exactly what changed in response -- a delta, not a full rebuild of the first deck. That keeps the conversation focused on confirming their feedback was addressed, not buried in a second pass through problem, options, and design as if the first review never happened. That's this chapter's whole arc: structure the argument, anticipate the questions, defend tradeoffs made on purpose, and revise under real feedback without losing why the design looked the way it did -- exactly what the Chapter 8 capstone asks you to do end to end.
